The Perses algorithm does allow removing non-leaf nodes, promoting children). The description says "Never remove the root, a required symbol, or a node with retained children." That suggests that if a node has children that are not removed, you cannot remove it. That seems contradictory to standard tree pruning where you can remove an internal node and promote its children. Maybe they mean "a node that has children that are retained" i.e., that node's children will remain in the final tree (so the node itself is a parent of retained children, so you cannot remove it because that would disconnect those children? So why prohibit? Possibly because the algorithm considers removal of nodes only if they have no retained children (i.e., leaf nodes or nodes whose entire subtree is removed). But Perses can remove interior nodes. The description also says "Consider deeper parse-tree nodes before shallower nodes." That suggests a bottom-up approach: we try to remove deeper nodes first. Typically in Perses, you visit nodes in post-order (children before parent). So you consider removing leaf nodes first, then if leaf removal is possible, then maybe interior nodes. But the condition "node with retained children" would prevent removing a node that still has children after some removals? Actually if you remove children first, then the parent may become a leaf (all children removed), then it's removable. So they likely mean you cannot remove a node that currently has children in the current state. So we should simulate the reduction process: repeatedly consider nodes in order (deeper first, tie by ID) that are removable and not root and not required symbol, and try to remove them if after removal all required symbols are still represented in the tree. If removal is allowed, we remove it (i.e., mark it removed) and its children become children of its parent. Then continue. After no more removals possible, the remaining nodes are retained.
